In [[cryptography]], '''PKCS #7''' ("PKCS #7: Cryptographic Message Syntax", "CMS") is a standard syntax for storing signed and/or encrypted data. PKCS #7 is one of the family of standards called Public-Key Cryptography Standards ([[PKCS]]) created by [[RSA Laboratories]].

==Standard==
The latest version, 1.5, is available as RFC 2315.<ref name="RFC2315">{{IETF RFC|2315}} – Public-Key Cryptography Standards (PKCS) #7: Cryptographic Message Syntax Specification Version 1.5, March 1998</ref>

An update to PKCS #7 is described in RFC 2630,<ref name="RFC2630">{{IETF RFC|2630}} – Cryptographic Message Syntax, June 1999</ref> which was replaced in turn by RFC 3369,<ref name="RFC3369">{{IETF RFC|3369}} – Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), August 2002</ref> RFC 3852<ref name="RFC3852">{{IETF RFC|3852}} – Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), July 2004</ref> and then by RFC 5652.<ref name="RFC5652">{{IETF RFC|5652}} – Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), September 2009</ref>

PKCS #7 files may be stored both as raw [[X.690|DER]] format or as [[Privacy-Enhanced Mail|PEM]] format. PEM format is the same as DER format but wrapped inside [[Base64]] encoding and sandwiched in between {{samp|{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}BEGIN&nbsp;PKCS7{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}}} and {{samp|{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}END&nbsp;PKCS7{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}{{nbhyph}}}}. Windows uses the <code>.p7b</code> file name extension<ref name=".p7b">{{Cite web|url=https://extension.nirsoft.net/p7b|title=.p7b Extension – List of Windows programs that can open .p7b files}}</ref> for both these encodings.

A typical use of a PKCS #7 file would be to store certificates and/or [[certificate revocation list]]s (CRL).

Here's an example of how to first download a certificate, then wrap it inside a PKCS #7 archive and then read from that archive:
<syntaxhighlight lang="console">
$ echo '' | openssl s_client -connect example.org:443 -host example.org 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 > example.org.cer 2>/dev/null

$ openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile example.org.cer -out example.org.cer.pem.p7b

$ openssl pkcs7 -in example.org.cer.pem.p7b -noout -print_certs
subject=C = US, ST = California, L = Los Angeles, O = Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, OU = Technology, CN = www.example.org issuer=C = US, O = DigiCert Inc, CN = DigiCert SHA2 Secure Server CA
</syntaxhighlight>

== File types ==
* <code>.p7r</code> – response to CSR. Contains the newly signed certificate, and the CA's own cert.
* <code>.p7s</code> – Digital Signature. May contain the original signed file or message. Used in [[S/MIME]] for email signing. Defined in RFC 2311.
* <code>.p7m</code> – Message (SignedData, EnvelopedData) e.g. encrypted ("enveloped") file, message or MIME email letter. Defined in RFC 2311.
* <code>.p7c</code> – degenerated SignedData "certs-only" structure, without any data to sign. Defined in RFC 2311.
* <code>.p7b</code> – SignedData structure without data, just certificate(s) bundle and/or [[revocation list|CRLs]] (rarely) but not a private key. Uses [[Distinguished Encoding Rules|DER]] form or [[X.690#BER_encoding|BER]] or PEM that starts with {{code|-----BEGIN PKCS7-----}}. The format used by Windows for certificate interchange. Supported by Java but often has <code>.keystore</code> as an extension instead. Unlike <code>.pem</code> style certificates, this format has a ''defined'' way to include certification-path certificates.
